searches.note: Thirty one searches of a share of forty five, none of them the author's, fourteen left unspent for the run's shared allowance. The three shared searches went to the law (Decreto-Lei 13/92 and Portaria 118/2014 on the Diário da República, for 1907, 1908 and the 85 and 67 per cent rules) and to the CVR Península de Setúbal's own page on Moscatel making and serving. Two searches were restricted to a house's own domain (ermelindafreitas.pt and horaciosimoes.com, read as primary through their summaries); every other search blocked the author's sources (the house where the account had to be independent, Wikipedia, Infopédia, 1001 Vinhos, Radar Wine, Vinha, Portugal Global, The Wine Society, the Évora thesis). Writers' own sites and addresses with a living name were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the law and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to what the stories turn on (the founder of 1834 and Periquita, the palace of 1528 and its tiles, the planting of 1974, the line of women of 1920, the revival claim of Moscatel Roxo, the charter of 1958 and the colony), then to the making of each flagship against listings the author had not read.

Where a fact rested only on merchants' sheets that read alike it was cut (old vines, fifty years, twenty days); where listings disagreed by vintage the line was widened and tied to the vintage (the Bacalhôa barrel time, the Pegões blend and oak); where a house's own claim met independent accounts that told it otherwise, the claim was kept only as the house's and taken out of the spoken line (the Moscatel Roxo revival).

tested: The founder, the house's domain blocked: born in 1804 in the Dão (Forbes, Restos de Colecção, which gives Vilar Seco and 31 May), a mathematics graduate of Coimbra (two accounts); 1834 and Vila Nogueira de Azeitão in every account read. His death is 1884 on Showcaves as on the house's timeline, so the author's choice to describe him stands.

Periquita, the house blocked: first sold in 1850 from the Cova da Periquita, bought near Azeitão in the 1840s (Forbes, Sipping Portugal, Cellar Tours and others); the claim of Portugal's first bottled red is the trade's and is not in the record. Borne out.

Alambre: the estate where the founder first planted Moscatel and the nod to amber are the house's own account, repeated by merchants; one mirror notes it is unconfirmed, so the story now hedges it as the label already did. The house's 2019 sheet (its own domain, read through the search) gives clay limestone and sandy soils, the fermentation stopped with aguardente vínica and three months on the skins, DOC Moscatel de Setúbal: the making and the sites borne out.

The Torna Viagem, the house blocked: the revival of 2000 with the Navy aboard the Sagres in Agroportal, Grande Consumo, Grandes Escolhas, Echoboomer, the CVR's news and an IVV notice, with later voyages to the ninth of 2026. Borne out; the nineteenth century trade stays the house's telling, as the story says.

Lancers, Wikipedia blocked: launched in 1944 at the request of an American importer, by the brand's own timeline and Sea and See Tours; a lightly sparkling rosé in a stoneware bottle. Borne out; Wikipedia replaced by the brand's page.

The old wines: the Moscatel de Setúbal Superior 1911 was made for the 180th anniversary and first offered at a launch auction in 2014 (the house's page, Agroportal, Garrafeira Nacional); the Moscatel Roxo Superior 1918 has its own sheet and a launch of 2018. The story said the house keeps them; now it says it released them. Prices met on merchants' pages were not used.

The shared searches went to the law: the decree of 10 May 1907, confirmed on 1 October 1908, by Decreto-Lei 13/92, which itself held the 85 per cent rule for the traditional names; Portaria 118/2014 restates it with 67 per cent for plain Setúbal. The CVR's page gives serving temperatures of 10 to 12 degrees Celsius as an aperitif and 12 to 14 for wines over five years; the house's own 10 to 16 for Alambre stands as its sheet.

The questions: one key each, four steps of making and four customs of fortified wine; the explanations teach why the nearest option is wrong. The house rules: nobody living named (the house's winemaker of today and a chef of the 2026 voyage met and not used), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.was: The house carries the name of its founder, a mathematician from the Dão, born in 1804 and trained at Coimbra, who settled at Vila Nogueira de Azeitão and there, in 1834 by the house's account, set up the company. By its own timeline he created its Moscatel de Setúbal brand in 1849, and he bought land across the peninsula, among it the Cova da Periquita, whose red was certainly being made by 1850. The house tells how, in the nineteenth century, merchant ships carried its Moscatel in cask to Brazil, Africa and India, and how the casks that came back unsold had improved on the voyage: the Torna Viagem, the wine of the return. In 1907 the Setúbal region was delimited for its Moscatel, and in 1944 the house created Lancers, a lightly sparkling rosé. In 2000 it revived the old voyage aboard the Sagres, the navy's training ship, comparing the travelled casks with casks kept at Azeitão, and it repeated the voyage in the years that followed. Among its special wines it keeps a Moscatel de Setúbal Superior of 1911 and a Moscatel Roxo of 1918. Alambre, named for the estate where the founder first planted Moscatel, is the house's plain statement of the style: months on the skins after fortification, then old wood.

tested: The palace, Infopédia and the Portuguese Wikipedia blocked: the estate sold in 1528 to Brás de Albuquerque (1500 to 1581, by one study), the only son of Afonso de Albuquerque (Pássaro no Ombro, the French Wikipedia, the tile studies), who had a Renaissance palace built; the gate inscribed 1554; the Susanna and the Elders panel dated 1565 in the central room of the pavilion by the lake (two technical studies of the azulejos, the state heritage register). The loggia was wrong and the eldest son loose: both fixed.

The name: in 1609 the estate passed to an heiress whose husband, a commander of the India fleet, was nicknamed o Bacalhau (Pássaro no Ombro, a blog of the monarchy's history); the French Wikipedia places him in the late sixteenth century, so only in the seventeenth century was cut. One travel blog tells a cod fisherman's legend instead; the record keeps the nickname as the story goes.

The American buyer: 1936 (Jornal de Negócios, Pássaro no Ombro) or 1937 (another account); the 1930s stand. Her grandson, then the owner, asked the head of João Pires to plant the vineyard (the company's Asian site, a Portuguese article); the first wine was sold among friends of that founder of João Pires and J.P. Vinhos (Grandes Escolhas). The engineer became the head of João Pires.

The planting and first vintage: 1974 and 1979 in Grandes Escolhas, Portugal Resident, Vinha and the company's sheets, which word the claim as the first Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot made in Portugal; 1972 on the company's Asian page and one Portuguese article with fourteen hectares and Petit Verdot, left open.

The company: João Pires & Filhos of 1922 in the centenary press (SAPO, Margem Sul, Hipersuper); one magazine says it was founded in the Algarve and moved to Setúbal in 1966, so the story names no place and no bulk trade; 1998 as the year of its principal shareholder, who is living and never named; Caves Aliança in 2007 by Hipersuper, the CVRA's page, Correio da Manhã and both Wikipedias.

The wine: no listing gives the nine tenths, so the great majority; cuvaison two weeks (Vinha) or three (Portugal Vineyards), not a week; new French oak for 11 (Portugal Vineyards), 13 (Vinha, Cellar Tours) or 24 months (Garrafeira Pepe) on the 2021 and 2022, at least six months in bottle; sandy loam and the Atlantic on Vinha; 16 to 18 degrees Celsius on most listings. Palácio da Bacalhôa: made from 2000 to mark the century and the purchase of the palace, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petit Verdot in new French oak (the company's sheets for the 2013, 2014 and 2016). The others line's thirty year Superior was not found and is cut.

The questions: one key each, four blends of Portuguese reds and four years; the lint's note on the first vintage is a question of a date, not a claim of a first, and stands. The house rules: the principal shareholder and the grandson met and not named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.was: The palace that gives the company its name stands at Vila Fresca de Azeitão: a Renaissance house built after 1528 for the eldest son of the conqueror of Goa, its loggia lined with tile panels, one of them dated 1565. The name came only in the seventeenth century, from Bacalhau, the nickname of an heiress's husband, as the story goes. The company began apart from it, in 1922, as João Pires & Filhos, a family firm making wine in bulk. In the 1930s an American woman bought the palace and restored it, and in 1974, at the request of the palace's owners, an engineer planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot beside it, and the company made its wine. Its first vintage, 1979, was by the company's account the first Portuguese Cabernet Sauvignon, a red of Bordeaux grapes on a peninsula of Castelão and Moscatel. The firm traded as J.P. Vinhos; from 1998 it had new owners, it later took the palace's name as Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal, and around the turn of the millennium the palace and its quinta were bought as well, with a second red named for the palace. In 2007 the company added Caves Aliança in the Bairrada. Quinta da Bacalhôa remains its founding statement: Cabernet on the peninsula, aged in new French oak.
changed.now: The palace that gives the company its name stands at Vila Fresca de Azeitão. The name came later, from Bacalhau, the nickname of an heiress's husband, as the story goes. The company began apart from it, in 1922, as João Pires & Filhos, a family firm. In the 1930s an American woman bought the palace and restored it, and in 1974, at the request of her grandson, the head of João Pires planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot beside it, and his firm made the wine. Its first vintage, 1979, was by the company's account the first Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot made in Portugal, a red of Bordeaux grapes on a peninsula of Castelão and Moscatel. The firm traded as J.P. Vinhos; from 1998 it had new owners, it later took the palace's name as Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal, and around the turn of the millennium the palace and its quinta were bought, with a second red named for the palace. In 2007 the company added Caves Aliança in the Bairrada. Quinta da Bacalhôa remains its founding statement: Cabernet on the peninsula, aged in new French oak.
changed.why: The son, not the eldest son; sold in 1528, then made a Renaissance palace; the 1565 panel is Susanna and the Elders in the lake pavilion; the nickname's century uncertain; the bulk trade unfound; the planter was the head of João Pires at the owner's grandson's request; the claim of a first worded as the company's sheets word it.

changed.was: Casa Ermelinda Freitas dates from 1920 at Fernando Pó, on the sandy plain of Palmela, and its line has run through the women of the family. The men died young, as the family tells it, and the farm passed from mother to daughter, from the founder to her daughter and then to the granddaughter for whom the house is named. For almost eighty years it sold its wine in bulk. That third woman, widowed when her husband died, kept the vineyards going with her daughter's help, and in the 1990s, after her father's death, the daughter came home from a career in social services and took the house in hand. She chose bottles over bulk, and the house began to sell its wine under its own labels, the range named for her mother, Dona Ermelinda, among them. Castelão has stayed at the heart of the vineyard, the grape of the Palmela DOC on sand, and the Dona Ermelinda Reserva blends that old vine Castelão with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon and gives it about a year in French oak. In 2020 the house marked a hundred years of wine. For a sommelier the Reserva is the Palmela of a family house: Castelão from the sand, made by the fourth generation of a house of women.
changed.now: Casa Ermelinda Freitas dates from 1920 at Fernando Pó, on the sandy plain of Palmela, and its line has run through the women of the family, from the founder to her daughter and then to the granddaughter for whom the house is named. For almost eighty years it sold its wine in bulk, for others to bottle. That third woman was widowed early and kept the vineyards going with her only daughter's help, and in the late 1990s the daughter left a career in social work in the health service and took the house in hand. She chose bottles over bulk, and the house began to sell its wine under its own labels, the range named for her mother, Dona Ermelinda, among them. Castelão has stayed at the heart of the vineyard, the grape of the Palmela DOC on sand, and the Dona Ermelinda Reserva blends it with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon and gives it about a year in French oak. In 2020 the house marked a hundred years of wine. For a sommelier the Reserva is the Palmela of a family house: Castelão from the sand, made by the fourth generation of a house of women.

tested: 1910, the founder and Quinta do Anjo, Vinha and the house's home page blocked: Garrafeira da Alvalade (founded by José Carvalho Simões in 1910, third generation), Wine House Portugal and The Wine Detective (third generation, 1910), and the house's Generosos page read through a search on its own domain. Borne out; the founder's dates were found nowhere, so he stays described.

The revival: the house's own pages say it backed a vine that had nearly disappeared from the region and revived it for this sweet wine. Público and Grandes Escolhas, read through one search, tell the vine's near loss to birds and early ripening and credit its survival to Bacalhôa, which held the last two hectares about twenty years ago, and to José Maria da Fonseca, whose Moscatel Roxo rosé helped save it; José Maria da Fonseca has released a Moscatel Roxo Superior of 1918. No account read gives Horácio Simões a part. The record keeps the claim only as the house's own and takes it out of the table line.

The vine: a colour mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, Muscat à Petits Grains, by Plantgrape (Moscatel Galego Roxo its Portuguese synonym) and a genetic study of Moscatel Galego's skin colour, with Wines of Portugal; the Muscat of Alexandria is Moscatel Graúdo in the VIVC list. Borne out; roxo means purple, so the trap now says so.

The rule: Decreto-Lei 13/92 already allowed the traditional names Moscatel de Setúbal and Roxo only at 85 per cent of the must, and Portaria 118/2014 restates it; the story's 2009 is now 1992 and restated since.

changed.was: The Setúbal peninsula was delimited for its Moscatel in 1907, and in 1910, by the house's own account, its founder began Casa Agrícola Horácio Simões at Quinta do Anjo, in the municipality of Palmela; three generations of the family have run it since. It makes the peninsula's range, Moscatel de Setúbal among its reds and whites, and its own pages speak of a policy of backing new products, one above all: Moscatel Roxo, a pink skinned Muscat that had all but disappeared from the region when the house chose to make it. Wines of Portugal describes the vine as thought to be a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, the small berried Muscat, and so a different vine from the Muscat of Alexandria behind ordinary Moscatel de Setúbal. The rules of the designation, set out again in 2009, allow the name Moscatel Roxo only when that grape gives at least 85 per cent of the must. The house's Moscatel Roxo is made in the Setúbal way, fortified and then left for months on its skins, and finished in used French oak barrels, and the house also keeps older bottlings of it. For a sommelier it is the pink Muscat in a family's hands: a rarer vine than the peninsula's own Moscatel, which this house, by its own account, chose to bring back.

changed.was: Adega de Pegões grew out of a settlement scheme. The state's Junta de Colonização Interna, created in 1936, chose the Herdade de Pegões, estates a brewing magnate had given to Lisbon's hospitals, and in the 1950s built an agricultural colony there: houses, land and vines for settler families from across the country, with its own church of Santo Isidro. The Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões received its charter on 7 March 1958 to serve those settlers, taking in their grapes and making their wine with the state's financial and technical help. After the revolution of 1974 it was taken over, and by its own account it went through years of upheaval in 1975 and 1976 before a long modernisation of its cellars, its fermentation vats and its bottling lines. Trading as Adega de Pegões, it makes red, white and fortified wines from its members' vineyards on the sandy plain, and its Colheita Seleccionada, made red and white, is a label its merchants abroad have listed vintage after vintage. The white blends Fernão Pires with Verdelho, Antão Vaz, Chardonnay and Arinto, fermented in oak and stirred on its lees. For a sommelier Pegões shows the peninsula's co-operative side: the grapes of many settler families, made in one cellar and sold under one name.
